summary: Fresh independent read-only review of the 261-file pinned working-tree subject relative to 3b50f1b identified four supported findings: destructive cleanup after an uncertain metadata commit, a PostgreSQL token-revocation lock-order race, unnecessary inline-body loading in framework state, and malformed display filenames breaking downloads. The focused 150-test suite passed; isolated fixtures confirmed the first, third and fourth mechanisms. All pinned source hashes matched before and after the review.
coverage: Read the complete immutable review-brief.txt, review-source.json pins, CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, project/workflow/invariants/review context, the evidence-file task and milestone 2 scope, and adversarial-review result contract. Reviewed the current tracked diff against base 3b50f1b and new untracked runtime/test source directly without implementation-worker conclusion artifacts.

Inspected apps/server/src/app.ts evidence schemas, multipart/detail/download/review routes, authentication/capability middleware and post-I/O evidenceAccess; apps/server/src/context.ts blob adapter ownership; evidence-http.ts bounds, cancellation, concurrency and download disposition.

Inspected all apps/server/src/blobs files: checked tenant/workspace/random-id references, SHA-256 verification, input copies, local private-path/symlink/hardlink/special-file handling and fd lifetime, S3 signed requests, streamed bounds, retries, deadlines, cleanup and client destruction.

Inspected services/evidence.ts and services/visua.ts file creation/download/review/edit, audit/event publication, workspace locking, inline hashing, score reads and agent/proposal dependencies. Traced storage/store.ts evidence metadata/body hydration and atomic writes/deletes; migration 6 preservation, rollback and migration locking; SQLite/PostgreSQL transaction drivers; auth token/session/membership dependencies; views, exports and SOC 2 evidence consumers.

Inspected packages/core/src/types.ts and evidence.ts approval/date/scope contracts, status/scoring dependencies, and core evidence tests. Inspected EvidencePage.tsx, UploadEvidence.tsx, RequirementPicker.tsx, lib/api.ts, workspace/query/auth dependencies, inspector evidence consumers, fixed detail snapshots, drafts, roles, stale callbacks and error/retry controls.

Read new blob-store, evidence-content, evidence-files and browser evidence-files test cases, and changes to evidence-binding tests. Ran env -u VISUA_TEST_DATABASE_URL pnpm exec vitest run apps/server/test/blob-store.test.ts apps/server/test/evidence-content.test.ts apps/server/test/evidence-files.test.ts apps/server/test/evidence-binding.test.ts packages/core/test/evidence.test.ts --reporter=dot from /Users/artem/visua: 5 files and 150 tests passed on SQLite, local/memory adapters and isolated signed mock-S3 HTTP.

Ran ignored isolated in-memory fixture data/review-fixtures/evidence-files-check.ts: injected a durable metadata transaction followed by a lost acknowledgement error and observed retained metadata/audit with deleted blob; accepted an unpaired-surrogate fileName edit then observed URIError in evidenceDisposition; recorded frameworkState joining evidence_content for a metadata-only count. Fixture output is in data/review-fixtures/evidence-files-check.log; focused suite summary is in data/review-fixtures/evidence-files-focused-tests.log.

Computed SHA-256 for every one of the 261 files declared by review-source.json before and after inspection/checks; no mismatches. Immutable review-brief.txt SHA-256: cb8c945fc736dfaac73ac32b1b0d9c01c3b6731758d5abed4f81ecd60614a45c. Runtime source was preserved; writes were limited to the requested JSON reports and ignored isolated fixture/log files.

findings.mechanism: The catch surrounding the metadata/audit transaction always deletes the uploaded blob. A PostgreSQL COMMIT can become durable while its acknowledgement is lost on a disconnected client, causing store.atomic/mutate to reject despite the evidence row and collected audit already being published. This cleanup then deletes the file referenced by committed metadata. Retrying cannot recover those original bytes and creates another item instead.
findings.evidence: createFileEvidence awaits this.mutate, then its catch calls this.blobs.delete(scope, reference.id) without proving the metadata transaction rolled back. PostgresDriver awaits COMMIT before returning and propagates query/connection failure. The isolated fixture wrapped the actual SQLite transaction to commit successfully then throw a simulated acknowledgement error: createFileEvidence rejected, committed_evidence_count=1, committed_evidence_audit_count=1, audit_chain_valid=true, and getEvidenceFile failed not_found. This executes the cleanup mechanism; actual PostgreSQL network loss was not injected.
findings.recommendation: Only delete a blob while publication is provably not attempted or provably rolled back. Once metadata publication begins, retain bytes on an uncertain transaction outcome, or reconcile with authoritative committed metadata before any deletion. Prefer retaining an unpublished object to deleting a possibly published artifact; leave orphan lifecycle policy to the later operational package. Add a commit-succeeded/acknowledgement-failed regression.

findings.mechanism: The new post-I/O authorization callback takes the tenant advisory lock before resolving a bearer token, but resolveApiToken can update last_used_at and acquire the token row lock. Revocation takes that row lock first and then waits for the tenant advisory lock in audit. If initial authentication sees last_used_at just under 60 seconds old and blob I/O crosses the refresh threshold, a concurrent revocation can hold the row while evidenceAccess holds the tenant lock, creating a PostgreSQL deadlock. PostgreSQL must abort one request; if it chooses revocation, the administrator's revoke operation rolls back and the token remains active.
findings.evidence: evidenceAccess explicitly awaits store.lock(ws:tenantId), then auth.resolveApiToken. resolveApiToken reads byHash and awaits apiTokens.touch when the timestamp exceeds 60,000 ms; touch executes UPDATE api_tokens. revokeApiToken executes apiTokens.revoke (UPDATE the same row) before this.audit, which calls svc.log and acquires the same ws:tenantId advisory lock. The ordinary SELECT in byHash can see the pre-revocation row while the competing revocation transaction is uncommitted, then its UPDATE waits on that transaction. This is a source-derived interleaving; PostgreSQL execution was reserved to root.
findings.recommendation: Use one lock order for token revocation and post-I/O evidence authorization, for example acquire the tenant lock before updating the revoked token row. Alternatively make the under-lock fresh token check side-effect free so it cannot touch last_used_at. Add a bounded PostgreSQL concurrent revoke/recheck regression with last_used_at crossing the minute threshold.

findings.mechanism: The ordinary framework state route still calls the hydrated evidence.list method even though it only needs metadata to calculate evidence counts. After migration 6 this joins and parses every inline artifact body for every framework state refresh, bypassing the intended metadata/content separation on the 3D scoring/state hot path. Large existing inline content therefore continues to incur full body reads and allocations despite svc.score itself using metadataList.
findings.evidence: frameworkState uses evidence only through isEvidenceValid and requirementIds at line 155. EvidenceCollection.list selects both e.data and c.data from evidence_content and readJoined hydrates body JSON. In the isolated fixture an inline artifact was inserted, frameworkState was called, and its recorded SQL included SELECT e.data AS metadata, c.data AS body ... LEFT JOIN evidence_content. This route requires no artifact content and remains body-dependent even when the score is cached.
findings.recommendation: Use metadataList in frameworkState and other consumers that only count/filter metadata. Preserve explicit hydrated content consumers separately. Extend the no-body-query regression to the framework state route, not only the svc.score method.

findings.mechanism: A JSON metadata edit can persist a fileName containing an unpaired UTF-16 surrogate, because the display-label validation checks length, paths and control characters but not Unicode well-formedness. evidenceDisposition passes that value to encodeURIComponent, which throws URIError. Subsequent downloads of an otherwise valid artifact return the generic 500 error until the name is corrected.
findings.evidence: The isolated fixture created file evidence, successfully called updateEvidence with fileName broken\ud800.bin, and then evidenceDisposition(changed.fileName) threw URIError: URI malformed. The file route invokes evidenceDisposition after obtaining verified bytes; the app's error handler maps this unrecognized URIError to 500. Multipart File names normally undergo scalar conversion, but the PATCH JSON schema accepts this string directly.
findings.recommendation: Reject non-well-formed Unicode labels or normalize the display filename to well-formed Unicode before RFC 5987 encoding. Make the disposition helper total for persisted display labels and add a focused filename/download regression.

limitations: Full pnpm check, PostgreSQL execution, Playwright/browser execution and live Docker/provider access were reserved to the integration owner and were not run by this reviewer. Browser tests were inspected, and the focused runtime suite used disposable SQLite plus local/signed mock-S3 fixtures.

The uncertain-commit fixture simulates a durable SQL transaction followed by a transport acknowledgement error; it establishes the destructive cleanup outcome but does not claim an actual PostgreSQL connection-loss experiment.
The token deadlock is established from the concrete row/advisory lock acquisition paths and timing condition; no PostgreSQL deadlock victim was observed in this review.

No claims are made about live provider policy, production throughput, backup/restore, or later retention, provenance, rejection-reason and supersession packages. Source pins were current at completion; subsequent implementation changes require a bounded review of their new inputs.
